Title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public

URL Source: https://www.techpolicy.press/the-sec-should-block-anthropics-ipo-to-protect-the-public/

Published Time: 2026-11-02T21:34:46.817Z

Markdown Content:
_Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report [Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts](https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/s/Brace-for-Impact-Scherer-Jenkins-OMI-October2026-WEB-1.pdf)._

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s [circular business dealings](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2026-ai-circular-deals/), extensive use of [financial engineering](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/opinion/ai-bubble-financial-crisis-lehman.html), and otherwise [murky finances](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-companies-hide-debt-off-balance-sheet) make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.

That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the [registration statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm) for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.

The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.

Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent [financial disclosures](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm) revealed [nearly $900 billion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/02/anthropic-ant-s-1-quarter-financials.html) in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth [slowed to a crawl](https://www.regenerator1.com/p/anthropics-growth-just-flattened) over the summer.

Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.

The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its [amended registration statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm#i199fd6a8a0664d5da497db9a78cf0452_271) reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.

Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts [in a legal and practical sense](https://www.ft.com/content/17a207f4-1563-48af-91e3-14bac89ab4b8?syn-25a6b1a6=1): they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.

Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate [further massive infrastructure and compute contracts](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/20/anthropic-nscale-data-center-deal.html), Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.

Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.

## Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins

AI industry margins

Demand pressure:

Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI.

Commoditization:

Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices.

Cost pressures:

High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash.

External constraints:

Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation.

First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple [studies](https://mlq.ai/media/quarterly_decks/v0.1_State_of_AI_in_Business_2025_Report.pdf), including from [organizations](https://www.deloitte.com/uk/en/issues/generative-ai/ai-roi-the-paradox-of-rising-investment-and-elusive-returns.html) notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are [not accelerating productivity](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/over-80-companies-report-no-151256180.html) or [otherwise generating positive returns on investment](https://www.apollo.com/wealth/insights-news/insights/daily-spark/no-signs-of-ai-payoff-outside-the-tech-sector) for [most businesses](https://www.chicagolandchamber.org/member-news/94-of-enterprise-ai-investments-fail-to-deliver-significant-roi-what-are-the-other-6-doing-differently/). Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work [fell significantly](https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2026/07/28/ai-revenues-are-growing-fast-but-not-fast-enough) between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).

Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in _paying_ for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was [tepid](https://www.ft.com/content/5ee49718-c258-4f01-aa32-7e5b76ae5245?syn-25a6b1a6=1).

#### Our content delivered to your inbox.

Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.

In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a [price war](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/the-ai-price-war-is-heating-upand-openai-is-gaining-ground-on-anthropic-48b8525b) this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts [further downward pressure](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/07/chinese-ai-models-costs-us-openai-anthropic.html) on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.

That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated [$31 billion](https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-ai-data-center-build-costs/), and the prices for some components are soaring.

That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company [estimates](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/anthropic-us-ai-needs-50gw-of-power-by-2028-frontier-models-will-require-5gw-data-centers/) it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.

And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.

Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to [AI in general](https://www.techpolicy.press/multiple-polls-find-most-americans-think-ai-is-moving-too-fast/) and [data centers in particular](https://www.washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/09/03/how-data-center-backlash-is-growing-us-statehouses/) across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.

Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.

If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already [historically overvalued](https://bsky.app/profile/did:plc:eba5pmrflumhle24v2d4hgen/post/3myatso3ak22w) and [disproportionately concentrated](https://bsky.app/profile/matthewus.bsky.social/post/3mydevga2g22h) in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created [a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash](https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/publications/report-brace-for-impact-protecting-people-and-the-economy-when-the-ai-bubble-burst); never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.

It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Title: Introducing LongCat-2.5

URL Source: https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5/

Markdown Content:
## LongCat-2.5 Native Multimodality for Agentic Tasks

2026-11-1

[GitHub Coming soon](https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5/)[HuggingFace Coming soon](https://longcat.ai/blog/longcat-2.5/)[Try it](https://longcat.chat/)[API Access](https://longcat.chat/platform/docs/)

We introduce LongCat-2.5, a native multimodal model for long-horizon agentic tasks. With 1.6 trillion total parameters and approximately 48 billion activated per token, it builds on LongCat-2.0 with stronger native visual understanding and agentic coding.

We incorporate more long-horizon trajectories into long-sequence training and use **large-scale long-horizon reinforcement learning** to strengthen end-to-end engineering capabilities across complex codebase development and full-project builds. We continue to scale this training pipeline through data synthesis, environment construction, and mixed training across harnesses. We also convert real-world agent failure trajectories into reproducible, verifiable training tasks, continually adding targeted training data to address model capability gaps.

LongCat-2.5 also represents visual signals as multi-level discrete tokens, enabling the backbone to process visual and textual inputs in a unified token-based format. Combining native visual understanding with agentic coding delivers **strong visual coding performance**, while also supporting creative design and 3D tasks.

These advances are supported by continued infrastructure improvements. We optimize long-context training and W4A4 inference on domestic AI accelerators, while numerical consistency between training and inference and long-context rollout optimizations enable efficient large-scale long-horizon RL.

## Metrics Dashboard

To provide a clear view of LongCat-2.5’s current capabilities, the charts below compare it with GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude-Opus-4.8, and Claude-Opus-5. Detailed evaluation results covering a broader set of models are presented in the table later in this post.

## Showcases

Every case below was generated end-to-end by LongCat-2.5, spanning software development and professional office scenarios — from real-time fluid simulation, 3D digital exhibitions, and city dioramas to business analysis, feedback reports, and event operations. Click any case to watch the full demo.

Software Development · Web Visual DEMO 01 / 08

Demo footage coming soon

Build a real-time fluid simulation and VFX tool with LongCat-2.5 that generates high-FPS, interactive webpages with live fluid dynamics, enabling developers, designers, and science communicators to visualize complex physical phenomena interactively and beautifully.

## Visual Primitive Modeling

LongCat-2.5 represents visual signals as multi-level discrete tokens, enabling the backbone to process visual and textual inputs in a unified token-based format. This design combines native-resolution visual tokenization, offline visual preprocessing, and visual embeddings learned jointly with the backbone, supporting native multimodal integration while simplifying visual computation and workload management during training.

**Discrete Native Resolution Vision Transformer:** To bring visual primitive modeling to a token-level abstraction analogous to language modeling, we represent visual signals as multi-level vocabulary tokens. We overcome the information bottleneck of visual discretization by applying Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) to native-resolution features from a Semantic-and-Aligned Encoder (SAE), as in [LongCat-Next](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27538).

Figure 1. Native-resolution visual tokenization: images at different resolutions are encoded as discrete token sequences and reconstructed by a visual de-tokenizer.

**Offline Visual Preprocessing:** To reduce online visual computation and workload heterogeneity, a fixed tokenizer allows visual token IDs to be precomputed and cached offline. The backbone therefore processes pretokenized sequences, simplifying long-sequence packing and partitioning and improving load balancing during distributed training.

**Native Visual Representation:** Visual codebook embeddings are learned jointly with the backbone. Preliminary validation on a smaller MoE model with approximately 3B activated parameters on average shows interwoven visual and textual embeddings in t-SNE visualizations, suggesting integration within a shared semantic space.

Figure 2. t-SNE comparison of visual and textual embeddings. The right panel shows validation on a MoE model with approximately 3B activated parameters on average.

## Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning

RL scaling is a key lever for pushing model intelligence further. For LongCat-2.5, we scale an end-to-end agentic RL pipeline across data, environments, algorithms, and harnesses for long-horizon tasks.

Figure 3. The agentic RL pipeline for long-horizon tasks, spanning data and environments, asynchronous training, reward design, and mixed training.

**Large-Scale Data Synthesis and Environment Construction:** For agentic tasks such as coding, the model learns from real environment feedback. A scalable synthesis pipeline automatically generates training tasks, interactive environments, and verifiable tests. We filter GitHub pull requests and linked issues, then use agents to annotate tasks and synthesize environments, validated with fail-to-pass (F2P) and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests. Real internal coding tasks and evaluation criteria broaden coverage of everyday engineering needs. Live rollout pass rates guide re-labeling and filtering, while offline analysis of false-positive and false-negative trajectories continually corrects and extends F2P tests to cover task specifications more fully and improve verification accuracy.

**Asynchronous RL and Stability:** To improve training efficiency, we adopt asynchronous partial rollouts: each RL step maintains an oversampling ratio, and once a full batch is collected, in-flight trajectories are interrupted, saved, and resumed in the next sampling phase. We increase oversampling based on precomputed pass rates and filter out zero-gradient groups whose rollouts all succeed or all fail, ensuring sufficient effective gradient signal. Tokens within one trajectory may be generated by different historical checkpoints, introducing staleness. We clip the discrepancy between sampling-policy and current-policy log-probs and rescale each token’s gradient contribution using accumulated historical discrepancy, bounding the gradient bias from staleness. Same-weight numerical differences are handled by the train–inference alignment described in the infrastructure section.

**Reward Hacking and Output Behavior:** We disable network access in task environments, remove git history and cached files, and use an LLM judge to audit trajectories for exploits, curbing opportunistic behavior. Additional penalties suppress repetitive reasoning and repeated tool calls during multi-turn interaction. To counter overthinking and overly rapid growth in response length, we redistribute reward among positive samples.

**Mixed Training and Generalization:** The model readily adapts to similar tasks and harnesses during RL. Only a small number of scaffold adaptation examples are needed in earlier training stages. During RL, we mix training tasks aligned with different benchmarks and scale their corresponding scaffolds in varying proportions. Mixed training across tasks and scaffolds improves generalization, with performance gains across tasks reinforcing one another.

## Learning from Multiple Teachers

To integrate specialized capabilities into the main model, we retain LongCat-2.0’s expert groups for agent capabilities, reasoning, and interaction, covering multi-turn task execution, single-turn reasoning, fine-grained instruction following, and safety without compromising usefulness. During MOPD, the student samples online across task domains, and domain experts train it through [full-vocabulary KL divergence](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash/blob/main/DeepSeek_V41_Tech_Report.pdf) on the sampled outputs.

Samples must reflect the student’s actual task behavior while allowing teachers to provide reliable signals. To limit distribution shift, prior work uses per-turn prefixes from trajectories seen by teachers during SFT or RL as contexts for student sampling. We further split each teacher response into fixed-length segments to form per-cut prefixes and cap student self-sampling at the same length to address distribution shift within long single-turn responses.

Figure 4. Per-cut prefixes for online student sampling.

To control computation and storage costs, prefixes from the same teacher trajectory are grouped on one inference engine, sharing prefill computation and KV cache. For training, we assemble a tree with the teacher trajectory as the trunk and student samples as branches. [Tree Attention](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.07606) completes OPD training for all samples in the group in one forward and backward pass, avoiding redundant computation and storage of the teacher trajectory.

## Long-Context Training on Domestic AI Accelerators

LongCat-2.5 uses long-sequence training during both mid-training and SFT. With less than 80 GB of memory per domestic AI accelerator, the training system prioritizes memory efficiency and aligns its parallelism with the supernode architecture.

### Supernode-Aware Parallelism

LongCat-2.5 aligns its parallel groups with the supernode topology, with FSDP and EP degrees equal to the number of accelerators per supernode and a CP degree no greater than that number. This keeps parameter all-gather, expert token all-to-all, and KV all-gather within the high-bandwidth supernode interconnect.

Hybrid vocabulary parallelism further reduces memory consumption by sharding the base embedding layer, LM head, and N-gram embeddings across the DP × CP domain.

To address load imbalance in large-scale expert parallelism, LongCat-2.5 introduces threshold-based dynamic expert replication built on MoonEP. Replication is only enabled when EP load imbalance reaches a configured threshold, avoiding communication overhead that outweighs the load-balancing gains, destination-side OOM caused by routed tokens, or sender-side OOM caused by communications.

The discrete image-token design simplifies parallelization by removing the vision encoder from the training graph. With image token counts known during data packing and shuffling, modality load ratios are predictable; this allows us to keep modality proportions approximately uniform across data-parallel ranks.

### FSDP and System Optimizations

LongCat-2.5 introduces dual-shard FSDP, which keeps model-parameter FSDP sharding within each supernode while further sharding FP32 master weights and optimizer states across FSDP domains through HSDP replicas, preserving efficient parameter communication and reducing persistent memory consumption.

Parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are organized into contiguous flattened buffers to support uneven sharding and Muon optimizer sharding, while direct weight-gradient writes and temporary-buffer reuse reduce intermediate copies and peak memory usage.

Zero-copy AllGather/ReduceScatter operations are involved to remove intermediate copies caused by default communication algorithms, while EP packs tokens and routing probabilities together for transmission and calls for AIV-based communication to alleviate AI-CPU task-expansion bottlenecks. Parameter prefetching overlaps all-gathers with computation while limiting contention with CP, and ScMoE overlaps EP communication with dense-branch computation.

Title: Preparing our next security sprint to harden OpenAI

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/preparing-our-next-security-sprint-to-harden-openai

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/preparing-our-next-security-sprint-to-harden-openai/

Markdown Content:
We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms.

We’re also [making improvements](https://openai.com/index/rewarding-defenders-with-bigger-bug-bounties/) to our[Security Bug Bounty program](https://openai.com/index/security-on-the-path-to-agi/) including more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them.

This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review.

We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.

Keeping the [defender’s window](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/) open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) customers. We’ve committed [$1 billion](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-for-frontline-defenders/) in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our [architecture and lessons⁠](https://openai.com/the-defense-factory/) from the last sprint, alongside our [blueprint](https://openai.com/index/empowering-cyber-defenders/) for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.

We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

articles.content:
U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation.
That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process.
Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising
a $31 million Series A
in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal.
The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity.
Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process.
The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company.
Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of  chips by the end of 2027.
The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up.
Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.”
AI companies once estimated
as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure
by 2030, but some investors have
grown skeptical of the buildout
, sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built.
“We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.”

Jay Peters

Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games,
as reported by
Tom’s Hardware
. Retro gaming is currently being overrun
with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports
, but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones.
Last week, a user on X
posted a screenshot
allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.”
Anthropic’s Addy Osmani,
in a reply
, didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5:
We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.
Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.
We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.
We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well.

OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters.

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
In
an announcement on Monday
, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.
The announcement comes as
opposition to data centers
spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah,
residents protested
after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.
Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”
Several states
like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to
moratoriums
and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as
a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC)
said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.
Related
Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
Who’s afraid of the big, bad GPU?
Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
OpenAI, which has switched to calling its
AI data centers “compute campuses”
in an effort to separate from their
poor public reputation
, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:
“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”
OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

Title: Goldman Sachs pulls AI coding tools from traders and bankers

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/goldman-sachs-pulls-ai-coding-tools-from-traders-and-bankers/

Published Time: 2026-11-02T20:00:03+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Goldman Sachs has cut off most of its employees from advanced AI coding tools like Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub.** Only engineers can still use them, according to [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-02/goldman-restricts-traders-and-bankers-from-using-some-ai-tools), citing internal guidelines from October. Traders and bankers had spent months using the tools to monitor trading flows and create content. The rollback is reportedly causing frustration inside the firm.

Back in July, [Goldman CIO Marco Argenti praised "vibe coding"](https://youtu.be/grOykIdJPgs?t=530) by non-technical staff in an interview. A trader or someone in asset management would have an idea, build a quick prototype with AI, and then hand it off to an engineer to scale for production. That's no longer the plan, it seems.

Why the U-turn? Bloomberg's report cites only a "variety of factors including productivity and risk management," according to Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra. He added that the experimentation phase is over, and the firm is now limiting the tools to the people "who are best suited to leverage them for the long term."

[Oracle](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/ORCL/) filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.

The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, [according to filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1341439/000119312526442729/d181425d424b5.htm) with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an [investor day last week](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/28/oracle-forecast-growth-2030.html), shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.

“This seems to be exactly what they previewed,” said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. “So I’m not sure why the market is freaking about it.”

Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.

Oracle’s one-day performance

The hyperscaler’s stock initially bounced after last Wednesday’s investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was [limiting its additional capital market funding](https://investor.oracle.com/investor-news/news-details/2026/Oracle-Investor-Day-2026-Accelerating-Value-Creation/default.aspx) for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.

“This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated),” UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.

Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.

Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.

The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle’s five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That’s more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence’s Gavan Nolan.

Oracle’s five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026

While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.

What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.

“Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space,” he said. “If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of ’27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out.”

_— CNBC’s Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting._

# Title:Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning

Authors:[Xinyan Hu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Hu,+X), [Pingbang Hu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Hu,+P), [Chloe Loughridge](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Loughridge,+C), [Xuanli He](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=He,+X), [Nicholas Carlini](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Carlini,+N), [Matthew Jagielski](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Jagielski,+M), [Javier Rando](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Rando,+J), [Yiming Zhang](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zhang,+Y)

View a PDF of the paper titled Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning, by Xinyan Hu and 7 other authors

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.37741)[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.37741v1)
> Abstract:Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at [this https URL](https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor).

In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.
Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT
Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:
Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver.
On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.
Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage.
At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.
Insufficient context reduces insight quality.
When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.
Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness.
At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.
Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights.
The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

Title: Anthropic’s growth just flattened (really)

URL Source: https://www.regenerator1.com/p/anthropics-growth-just-flattened

Published Time: 2026-10-15T15:07:23+00:00

Markdown Content:
Source: Regenerator estimates and news reports.

Anthropic shared high-level Q3 financials with investors yesterday, report [the NYT’s Andrew Ross Sorkin](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/14/technology/anthropic-ipo-revenue-profit.html), [Lauren Hirsch](https://www.nytimes.com/by/lauren-hirsch), and [Sri Muppidi](https://www.nytimes.com/by/sri-muppidi).

Revenue for Q3 was reportedly $16.8 billion.

At first glance, this number seems astonishing. And, in one sense, it is. It’s another jaw-dropping sequential gain for what is likely the fastest-growing company in history.

But, break the trend down into implied monthly growth, and the picture looks different.

Specifically, it seems Anthropic barely grew from July to September.

Anthropic’s sequential revenue growth in Q3, moreover, was smaller in absolute dollars than its (gobsmacking) growth in Q2.

So, for several possible reasons, Anthropic’s growth has meaningfully slowed.

This is likely another reason why the stocks of “neocloud” providers like CoreWeave are collapsing. CoreWeave, _et al_, have borrowed tens of billions of dollars on the assumption that demand for AI compute will continue to grow at rates way beyond consensus expectations for years.

Now, not only are interest rates soaring — raising the carrying costs of this debt — the near-term revenue growth for AI services may be flattening.

Anthropic’s reported revenue growth this year has been unprecedented:

**Q1:**$4.8 billion
**Q2:**$11.6 billion (+$6.8B and +141%, sequentially)
**Q3:** $16.8 billion (+$5.2B and +45%, sequentially)

Again, these numbers are astonishing.

But so are AI valuations and expectations.

Note that Anthropic added more revenue in Q2 than it did in Q3.

Note, too, that what matters most for Anthropic’s IPO valuation — and, likely, for the future trajectory of the AI bubble — is not what _has happened_ but what _will happen_.

The key question is, “What do these numbers suggest about how fast Anthropic will grow _from here_?”

These figures suggest that the market should temper its expectations, at least temporarily.

If we break down the quarterly figures above into monthly estimates and add one more reported data point — that Anthropic had a [$65 billion annualized revenue run-rate in July](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/17/anthropic-says-annualized-revenue-climbed-to-65-billion-in-july.html) —we see that Anthropic’s growth has flattened even more than the quarterly figures suggest.

Below are back-of-the-envelope estimates for Anthropic’s monthly revenue in 2026. They are based on the reported quarterly revenue figures as well as the $65 billion annualized revenue in July (which equates to ~$5.4 billion of July revenue).

Even the quarterly numbers suggest that Anthropic’s average monthly growth slowed from ~$760 million in Q2 to (“only”) $580 million a month in Q3.

But the “$65 billion annualized revenue in July” data point suggests the slowdown is even sharper.

If Anthropic did $5.4 billion in revenue in July and $16.8 billion in Q3, it likely only grew modestly in August and September.

According to DealBook, at its meeting with investors yesterday, Anthropic did _not_ share an annualized revenue number based on September’s revenue. This suggests — to this analyst, anyway — that Anthropic did not think the September annualized revenue figure would show impressive-enough growth versus July.

Indeed, when we extrapolate the monthly figures, it seems Anthropic saw a sharp change in its growth trajectory in August and September.

It means that the growth of the leading company in the sector appears to have slowed sharply in the past two months.

The slowdown might at least in part be the result of seasonality. August, at least, tends to be a slow month. But it’s early in a product cycle to see such sharp seasonality. And September’s growth should have sped back up.

It might also mean that Anthropic is simply not able to keep up with the growth of demand. If this is the reason for the slowdown, it’s a high-quality problem, and it won’t have a long-term impact on the overall AI spending growth trajectory (or bubble).

But it may also mean that the near-term growth rate of AI spending is moderating — either because demand growth is moderating or because companies are using cheaper models from China for some of their AI needs. (Usage data suggests the latter is in fact happening).

If _a slowdown in spending growth_ is the explanation, we should expect the wild investor enthusiasm for all things AI — and the colossal infrastructure spending growth supporting it — to also begin to moderate.

The [end of all bubbles comes](https://www.regenerator1.com/p/when-will-the-ai-bubble-burst) when supply begins to catch up with demand.

Anthropic’s apparent slowdown suggests we may be closer to reaching that moment.

**See Also:**[When will the AI Bubble burst? And why?](https://www.regenerator1.com/p/when-will-the-ai-bubble-burst)
